newsitem.title: GERMANY: Political meddling may threaten future Euro bank.
newsitem.headline: Political meddling may threaten future Euro bank.

text.p: The European Central Bank (ECB) will have a strong set of policy tools at its disposal, but economists say that meddlesome politicians could subvert the institution charged with steering Europe's monetary future.

In a new report on the ECB's operational framework, the European Monetary Institute revealed on Friday a set of policy-making tools for the future bank which will be broadly similar to those used to rigorous effect by the steely Bundesbank, Germany's central bank.

But observers said technicalities alone will not help the ECB withstand a potential onslaught of political pressure for a weaker euro after the single currency is launched in 1999 -- especially if jobless levels remain at their present highs.
"On paper, it all looks good," said Joachim Fels, economist at investment house Morgan Stanley in London.

"But the Bundesbank did not build its reputation on the fact that it had a Lombard rate or minimum reserves -- but rather on the fact that it was able to withstand pressure for a looser monetary policy," he added.
"The key question is -- will the ECB be able to fight political pressure for lower interest rates?".

Under the EMI's game plan -- which has to be approved by the ECB next year -- the new bank will conduct policy mainly through open market operations, with two further interest rates setting upper and lower limits for short-term rates.
Its overall strategy has yet to be finalised, but the EMI stressed that the ECB's primary objective will be -- like the Bundesbank's -- to maintain price stability.
Economists say such technical provisions should be more than adequate to allow the European Central Bank to operate a tight and accurate monetary policy -- but only in theory.
"The main problem is going to be the level of political interference in policy under monetary union," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs, Frankfurt.
"What the Bundesbank has done carefully over the years is deflect this tendency and this is what the ECB is up against if it wants to follow in its footsteps," Mayer added.

The EMI on Friday declined to comment on the risk of political interference on ECB policy, with its president Alexandre Lamfalussy simply noting that there had been no attempt from any quarter to curb the ECB's independence.

Economists said they were especially wary of recent proposals from France for a "stability council", a body comprising finance ministers and possibly other top politicians which would monitor developments in the euro area.
If such a body were given real legal powers on exchange rate policy, as has been mooted, economists fear it would deflect the ECB from its price stability goal.
"If this council is set up specifically to act as a political counterweight to the ECB, then of course the central bank would be restricted," Goldman Sachs's Mayer said.

"I personally think this (the stability council) is going to be the key issue in this whole European debate in 1997, like the stability pact was last year," said Darren Williams, European economist at UBS in London.

However, economists agreed that the ECB's credibility would be impossible to gauge accurately until it actually took over responsibility for monetary policy in the euro area, as planned for January 1999.
But even in the best-case scenario, the future European central bank is unlikely to match the Bundesbank's near-legendary decisiveness on policy right from the start.
"In Germany, a situation has developed that when it comes to monetary policy, politicans keep their hands off, but other countries have other habits and other ideas," Mayer said.

"People often say of the Bundesbank that it 'forms' its council members, no matter what region they come from or interests they represent. The ECB will have to develop this kind of 'corporate identity' too but whether it can do that is totally up in the air."
